BEFORE THE NEW MEXICO PUBLIC REGULATION COMMISSION

IN THE MATTER OF THE APPLICATION          )
OF EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY FOR           )

                   DIRECT TESTIMONY OF

                     RICHARD HANWAY

                       ON BEHALF OF

                  THE CITY OF LAS CRUCES

                             DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                              RICHARD HANWAY
                          NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT

                                       i
                                   DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                    RICHARD HANWAY
                                NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1   I.    INTRODUCTION

 2   Q.    PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.

 3   A.    My name is Richard Hanway and my business address is 300 Lohman Avenue, Las

 4         Cruces, New Mexico 88005.

 5

 6   Q.    WHAT IS YOUR CURRENT EMPLOYMENT?

 7   A.    I am employed as the Transit Director for the City of Las Cruces ("City").

 8

 9   Q.    HOW LONG HAVE YOU HELD YOUR CURRENT POSITION WITH THE

10         CITY?

11   A.    I have served as the City’s Transit Director since March 23, 2025.

12

13   Q.    PRIOR TO YOUR CURRENT POSITION AS THE CITY’S TRANSIT

14         DIRECTOR, DID YOU SERVE THE CITY IN OTHER ROLES?

15   A.    Prior to becoming the Transit Director, I was the Transit Operations Supervisor

16         and, before that, Transit Manager beginning in October 2015 and Transit Bus

17         Operator begin

18

19   II.   STATEMENT OF QUALIFICATIONS

20   Q.    PLEASE SUMMARIZE YOUR EDUCATION AND PROFESSIONAL

21         TRAINING.

22   A.    I earned a Bachelor of Science degree in Business Administration in 2004.

                                               1
                                  DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                   RICHARD HANWAY
                               NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


1    Q.   BEFORE JOINING THE CITY, WHAT EXPERIENCE AND TRAINING

2         DID YOU HAVE THAT IS RELEVANT TO YOUR CURRENT POSITION?

 3   A.   Prior to working with the City, I owned Hanway Trucking with my father from

 4        1996 to 2008., I was a driver, dispatcher, freight broker, and financier.

 5

 6   Q.   WHAT ARE YOUR CURRENT RESPONSIBILITIES WITH THE CITY’S

 7        TRANSIT DEPARTMENT?

 8   A.   I oversee Roadrunner Transit’s fixed route public transit operations and

 9        complementary para-transit operations. I am responsible for daily operations,

10        planning, grants, procurement, maintenance and upkeep of facilities and vehicles

11        and community engagement. I am a member of American Public Transit

12        Association (APTA), South West Transit Association (SWTA), New Mexico

13        Transit Association (NMTA), and I sit on the board for the Technical Advisory

14        Committee of the Mesilla Valley Metropolitan Planning Organization. I also work

15        closely with Center for Transportation and the Environment (CTE), one of the

16        largest advocates for low/no emission vehicles in public transit.

17

18   Q.   WHAT ROLES HAVE YOU PLAYED IN BRINGING TRANSPORTATION

19        ELECTRIFICATION TO THE CITY’S TRANSIT SERVICES?

20   A.   I started looking at battery electric buses in 2014. In 2015, bus OEM Build your

21        Dreams (BYD) loaned us one of their battery electric buses to use on our city routes

22        for a week. We collected data on energy use and range. Our drivers got to drive the

                                               2
                              DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                               RICHARD HANWAY
                           NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1   buses and test the technology and regenerative braking. In 2015, I first talked with

 2   El Paso Electric Company (EPE or Company) about Roadrunner possibly

 3   transitioning our diesel bus fleet to battery electric. I continued to learn about the

 4   technology. In 2017, I was part of the team to write a competitive grant proposal to

 5   the Federal Transit Administration. In 2017 we were awarded a Low & No

 6   Emission grant to purchase battery electric buses. Roadrunner was also awarded

 7   funding to build a new maintenance facility, where we would charge the buses.

 8            I had several conversations with EPE personnel regarding a rate structure

 9   for Las Cruces. At the time, there was no rate structure for charging vehicles in

10   southern New Mexico. We coordinated our bus build with EPE & BYD to deliver

11   buses once our new maintenance facility had chargers installed to charge the buses.

12   In April 2021, while EPE’s general rate case was pending, EPE communicated with

13   me about its proposed new Electric Vehicle Charging Rate No. 42 being expanded

14   to include customers with voltages up to 480 volts, so that Roadrunner could take

15   advantage of the new charging rates. Our facility had to put a separate meter to the

16   chargers, as was agreed upon with EPE, to receive service under Rate No. 42.

17            In 2022, Roadrunner was awarded another Low & No Emission grant to

18   replace six more diesel buses with battery electric buses. Our first five battery

19   electric buses went into service in August 2024, and our next six buses went into

20   service in May 2026. I continuously work with EPE personnel, discussing their

21   programs, rebates, and future growth of our vehicle transition to battery electric

22   buses.

                                           3
                                    DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                     RICHARD HANWAY
                                 NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1

 2   Q.     HAVE YOU EVER TESTIFIED BEFORE THE NEW MEXICO PUBLIC

 3          REGULATION COMMISSION PRIOR TO THIS CASE?

 4   A.     No, I have not previously testified before the New Mexico Public Regulation

 5          Commission (NMPRC or Commission).

 6

 7   III.   PURPOSES AND SCOPE OF TESTIMONY

 8   Q.     WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR TESTIMONY IN THIS CASE?

 9   A.     The City of Las Cruces’ rate design consultant, Justin Barnes, is providing expert

10          technical testimony about EPE’s proposed changes to EPE Rate No. 42, Electric

11          Vehicle Charging Service. The purposes of my testimony are to provide factual

12          background information about the City’s electric buses and transit services, to

13          explain the development of the City’s electric bus initiative in coordination with

14          negotiations with EPE and litigation before the New Mexico Public Regulation

15          Commission, and to describe the potential effect upon the City’s electric bus

16          program if the Commission were to adopt the changes to Rate No. 42 that EPE has

17          proposed in this general rate case.

18

19   IV.    THE CITY’S ELECTRIC BUS PROGAM AND FACILITIES

20   Q.     WHAT TYPES OF ELECTRIC BUSES DOES THE CITY UTILIZE?

21   A.     Currently, the Roadrunner Transit system owns and operates eleven full-size

22          electric buses serving eight routes throughout the city limits.     The hours of

                                                  4
                                   DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                    RICHARD HANWAY
                                NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1        operation are 6:30 a.m. through 10:30 p.m. Monday through Friday and 8:30 a.m.

 2        through 4:30 p.m. on Saturday. Since the COVID-19 pandemic, the City has

 3        chosen to provide bus service free of charge to users.

 4   B.

 5   Q.   WHEN DID THE CITY BEGIN USING ELECTRIC BUSES ON ITS

 6        ROADRUNNER TRANSIT ROUTES?

 7   A.   Our first five buses were placed into service in 2024, and six more were added in

 8        2026. However, the process of deciding to replace diesel buses with electric ones

 9        was long and complicated and dates back to 2015.

10

11   Q.   WHAT MOTIVATED THE CITY TO CONSIDER UTILIZING ELECTRIC

12        BUSES?

13   A.   There were numerous considerations, including the availability of federal funding,

14        the City’s broad goals for improving air quality, and the potential for cost savings

15        relative to the costs of operating diesel-fueled buses.

16

17   Q.   TO WHAT EXTENT WERE THE COST SAVINGS, OR COST

18        COMPARABILITY, IMPORTANT TO THE CITY’S DECISION TO

19        PURCHASE ELECTRIC BUSES?

20   A.   The City Transit department operates as an enterprise fund.           Cost-efficient

21        decisions are essential. Beginning in 2016, before we applied for the Low & No

22        Emission grant, we began meeting with the Center for Transportation and the

                                                5
                                  DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                   RICHARD HANWAY
                               NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1        Environment (CTE), a non-profit organization that provides technical assistance

 2        and guidance through the process of deploying zero-emission buses. There was no

3         electric utility charging rate then. Once we were award the first grant in 2017, we

4         started conversations with EPE to establish a vehicle charging rate for Southern

5         New Mexico. The Company modeled Rate No. 42 after a charging rate that they

6         had in place in Texas. We partnered with CTE to be our project manager for our

 7        bus build, charge rate modeling, and route block modeling. They also track

 8        performance of vehicles and chargers. They helped guide us with important

 9        questions to ask EPE regarding the rates they were proposing and what was

10        happening across the country. Comparing the costs of owning and operating diesel

11        buses with the costs of owning and operating electric buses naturally depends

12        greatly upon the projected costs of fuel (diesel or electricity). Therefore, EPE’s

13        then-available rates and potential electric vehicle charging rate structures were a

14        key element in the City’s decision making process.

15

16   V.   DEVELOPMENT OF EPE’S ELECTRIC VEHICLE CHARGING RATES

17   Q.   DID EPE HAVE A RATE SPECIFICALLY DESIGNED FOR ELECTRIC

18        VEHICLE CHARGING AT THE TIME THE CITY WAS INVESTIGATING

19        INVESTING IN ELECTRIC BUSES?

20   A.   No, it did not. However, the availability of federal funding of various types for

21        transportation electrification, including Federal Transportation Administration

22        (“FTA”) funding for public transit projects such as Roadrunner Transit and for

                                               6
                                   DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                    RICHARD HANWAY
                                NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1        personal electric vehicles; the availability of additional funding as a result of the

 2        Volkswagen settlement; passage of New Mexico’s transportation electrification

 3        statute, NMSA 1978, Section 62-8-12 in 2019, which required utilities to submit

 4        transportation electrification plans to the Commission; and recognition by electric

 5        utility providers that vehicle electrification would provide a new revenue stream,

 6        as indicated in EPE’s presentations concerning its upcoming Integrated Resource

 7        Plan, converged about the time that EPE filed its last general rate case application

 8        in NMPRC Case No. 20-00104-UT in May 2020.

 9

10   Q.   DID EPE PROPOSE AN ELECTRIC VEHICLE CHARGING RATE IN

11        CASE NO. 20-00104-UT?

12   A.   Yes, the Company proposed an “Experimental Electric Vehicle Charging Rate,”

13        Rate Schedule No. 42, in its application in Case No. 20-00104-UT. However, that

14        rate was limited to charging at 120 volts or 240 volts and, therefore, was not

15        available to the City for charging full-sized electric buses.

16

17   Q.   WAS THE CITY’S TRANSIT DEPARTMENT CONFERRING WITH EPE

18        WHILE ITS FORMAL PROPOSAL FOR A NEW ELECTRIC VEHICLE

19        CHARGING RATE WAS PENDING BEFORE THE COMMISSION?

20   A.   Yes, the Transit Department and its consultant CTE had been discussing electric

21        vehicle charging rates for the planned electric buses with EPE before the 2020

22        general rate case was filed and reached out to the Company not long after the

                                                7
                                  DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                   RICHARD HANWAY
                               NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1        specific proposed tariff was filed with the NMPRC. EPE’s filing of a proposed

 2        Rate No. 42 gave the City something concrete to analyze and discuss with CTE and

 3        with the Company. If it were to be available for charging the City’s buses, the

 4        economics of the electric bus procurement would improve, but Transit would have

 5        to devise patterns and schedules for charging its buses that would maximize the

 6        potential of low-cost super off-peak charging while accommodating Roadrunner

 7        route schedules that ended at 10:30 p.m. and began at 6:30 a.m. the following

 8        morning and while allowing for other maintenance and servicing of the buses. It

 9        was also necessary for Transit, with the help of CTE, to evaluate how best to handle

10        routes that could not be completed on a single daily charge and would require

11        additional charging before or after the high-priced afternoon on-peak period during

12        summer month weekdays.

13

14   Q.   OTHER THAN THE VOLTAGE LEVEL LIMITATION, DID THE CITY

15        HAVE CONCERNS ABOUT EPE’S PROPOSED RATE NO. 42 IN CASE

16        NO. 20-00104-UT?

17   A.   Yes, it did. The City was pleased that EPE had proposed a rate structure with a

18        high on-peak rate, a lower off-peak rate, and an extremely low super off-peak rate

19        to encourage vehicle charging during the early morning hours. The City also was

20        pleased that the proposed rate did not include a demand charge, as EPE’s demand

21        charges generally are applied to the customer’s highest monthly peak load at any

22        time of day or night. The City was concerned, however, about the basis for EPE’s

                                               8
                                   DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                    RICHARD HANWAY
                                NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1        calculation of the on-peak energy rate, which was higher than any on-peak energy

 2        rate proposed for other rate classes. The City also was concerned about EPE’s

 3        titling of the tariff as an “Experimental Electric Vehicle Charging Rate,” because

 4        of the implication that the duration and the terms were less certain than those of

 5        other Commission-approved tariffs. City witnesses José F. Provencio and Lisa

 6        LaRocque testified to these concerns, as well as discrepancies between the duration

 7        of the super off-peak period in the proposed tariff and supporting testimony, in the

 8        NMPRC proceeding. They urged that the voltage limitation be modified so that the

 9        City’s electric buses would be able to participate.

10

11   Q.   DID EPE ACCEDE TO THE CITY’S PRIMARY CONCERNS ABOUT THE

12        DURATION OF THE RATE NO. 42 SUPER OFF-PEAK PERIOD AND

13        MAKING EV CHARGING SERVICE AVAILABLE AT 480 VOLTS?

14   A.   Yes.   In rebuttal testimony in Case No. 20-00104-UT, EPE witness Manuel

15        Carrasco explained that his written testimony reflected EPE’s true intention to

16        establish a super off-peak period extending from 12:00 a.m. to 8:00 a.m. In

17        supplemental testimony filed in response to a bench request issued by the hearing

18        examiner, Mr. Carrasco testified that there were no substantive or technical reasons

19        why eligibility for Rate No. 42 could not be expanded to customers taking electric

20        service at up to 480 volts.

21

22   Q.   DID EPE LATER CHANGE ITS POSITION ABOUT RATE NO. 42?

                                                9
                                  DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                   RICHARD HANWAY
                               NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1   A.   Yes and no. EPE did not change its positions or withdraw its proposed Rate No.

 2        42 from Case No. 20-00104-UT.             However, shortly after Mr. Carrasco’s

 3        supplemental testimony was filed in that docket, and before the public hearing in

 4        Case No. 20-00104-UT, EPE filed its first Transportation Electrification Plan under

 5        the Transportation Electrification statute, NMSA 1978, Section 62-8-12, in

 6        NMPRC Case No. 20-00241-UT. In the Transportation Electrification Plan, the

 7        Company proposed a replacement Rate No. 42 that would have established

 8        different customer charges and energy rates for electric vehicle charging customers

 9        who otherwise would take service under EPE’s Residential Service Rate No. 1 and

10        under commercial service Rate Nos. 3, 4, and 9 and City/County service Rate No.

11        7. The version of Rate No. 42 proposed in Case No. 20-00241-UT also included

12        demand charges for all electric vehicle changing customers other than residential

13        customers.

14

15   Q.   HOW DID THE CITY REACT TO THE COMPANY’S SECOND

16        ELECTRIC VEHICLE CHARGING RATE PROPOSAL IN CASE NO. 20-

17        00241-UT?

18   A.   EPE’s application in Case No. 20-00241-UT was filed on December 30, 2020,

19        shortly before the hearing in the rate case was to begin. The City intervened in that

20        case at the beginning of April 2021, a few days before the hearing examiner’s

21        recommended decision was issued in Case No. 20-00104-UT. As the electric bus

22        procurement process was proceeding, the Company’s proposal to radically change

                                               10
                                  DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                   RICHARD HANWAY
                               NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1        an electric vehicle charging rate structure that had not even reached the point of a

 2        final decision by the Commission was confusing because we had not powered a

 3        single bus under the rate and there was no date to use to justify any changes at that

 4        time.

 5

 6   Q.   WHAT DID THE HEARING EXAMINER RECOMMEND REGARDING

 7        PROPOSED RATE NO. 42 IN THE GENERAL RATE CASE?

 8   A.   The recommended decision issued on April 6, 2021, in Case No. 20-00104-UT

 9        recommended that Rate No. 42 be made available to customers taking service at

10        voltages up to 480 kV—which would enable Transit to take advantage of the rate

11        structure. It also provided for a standard summer month on-peak period of 3:00

12        p.m. to 7:00 p.m., which was shorter than EPE’s proposed 1:00 p.m. to 7:00 p.m.

13        period. It set forth similar but recalculated Rate No. 42 rate components consistent

14        with the hearing examiner’s recommended overall revenue requirement and

15        approach to time-of-day rates.     Finally, the recommended decision set forth

16        numerous reporting requirements for EPE to enable analysis of the effectiveness

17        and design of Rate No. 42 in the Company’s next general rate case.

18

19   Q.   DID THE RECOMMENDED DECISION ADDRESS THE FACT THAT EPE

20        HAD A SECOND, DIFFERENT RATE NO. 42 PROPOSAL PENDING IN

21        CASE NO. 20-00241-UT?




                                               11
                                   DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                    RICHARD HANWAY
                                NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1   A.   The Case No. 20-00104-UT recommended decision did not explicitly address the

 2        possibility that the Company’s proposal in Case No. 20-00241-UT might supersede

 3        the Rate No. 42 proposal and critiques that were under consideration in the general

 4        rate case. However, in approving a new electric vehicle charging rate structure, the

 5        hearing examiner observed that the Transportation Electrification Plan application

 6        was not scheduled for a hearing for another three months and did not have a

 7        statutory deadline for completion, and that the City had expressed a need for electric

 8        vehicle charging within a matter of months.

 9

10   Q.   HOW DID THE CITY REACT TO THE RATE CASE RECOMMENDED

11        DECISION THAT WOULD ENABLE IT TO TAKE SERVICE UNDER AN

12        ELECTRIC VEHICLE CHARGING RATE WITH NO DEMAND

13        CHARGES AND A SUPER OFF-PEAK ENERGY RATE OPTION, WHILE

14        THE COMPANY WAS PROPOSING TO IMPOSE DEMAND CHARGES

15        AND OTHER CHANGES IN THE PENDING TRANSPORTATION

16        ELECTRIFICATION CASE?

17   A.   As previously mentioned, the City had intervened in Case No. 20-00241-UT. It

18        then submitted pre-filed direct testimony by Ms. LaRocque and Mr. Provencio

19        opposing the proposed Rate No. 42 tariff changes, particularly the demand charges

20        for non-residential electric vehicle charging customers. The City noted that since

21        2017, EPE’s Texas retail rates included an electric vehicle charging rate without

22        demand charges.

                                               12
                                  DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                   RICHARD HANWAY
                               NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1

 2   Q.   WHAT HAPPENED NEXT IN BOTH CASES?

 3   A.   During the period that the Commission was publicly debating the recommended

 4        decision in Case No. 20-00104-UT, EPE, NMPRC Staff, and several of the

 5        intervenors in Case No. 20-00241-UT reached a stipulation in which they agreed to

 6        remove demand charges from the proposed revision to Rate No. 42. The City

 7        opposed that stipulation, in part because it did not reflect the shortened on-peak

 8        period of 3:00 p.m. to 7:00 p.m. that the hearing examiner had recommended in

 9        Case No. 20-00104-UT. A couple of days after the City filed its statement in

10        opposition to the stipulation, the Commission approved the terms of Rate No. 42 as

11        set out in the recommended decision in Case No. 20-00104-UT.

12

13   Q.   WHERE DID THAT LEAVE RATE NO. 42 AND THE STIPULATION IN

14        CAST NO. 20-00241-UT?

15   A.   Two days after the rate case final order was issued, the hearing examiner in Case

16        No. 20-00241-UT determined that a hearing should be held on the contested

17        stipulation in Case No. 20-00241-UT and set a procedural schedule a few days later.

18        EPE witness Carrasco’s pre-filed testimony in support of the stipulation stated that

19        the billing demand provision of the revised Rate No. 42 originally proposed in Case

20        No. 20-00241-UT had been “inadvertently deleted” when the tariff schedule

21        attached to the stipulation was prepared. He attached to his testimony a new version




                                              13
                                   DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                    RICHARD HANWAY
                                NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1        of Rate No. 42 that restored that demand provision, which applied to electric service

 2        taken at all times other than during the super off-peak period.

 3

 4   Q.   HOW DID THE CITY RESPOND TO THAT TESTIMONY?

 5        Both Ms. Larocque and Mr. Provencio filed rebuttal testimony pointing out the

 6        inconsistency between the stipulation term agreeing to removal of demand charges

 7        from Rate No. 42 and Mr. Carrasco’s testimony reinserting such language. They

 8        questioned whether the stipulating parties truly were in agreement. The day after

 9        that testimony was filed, the hearing examiner ordered the stipulating parties to file

10        supplemental testimony in which they all attested to a shared understanding of the

11        stipulated tariff terms.

12

13   Q.   DID THE STIPULATING PARTIES EXPRESS AGREEMENT WITH MR.

14        CARRASCO’S NEW REVISIONS TO PROPOSED RATE NO. 42?

15   A.   No, they did not. Two days before the hearing on the stipulation, the stipulating

16        parties jointly filed testimony expressing their agreement that Mr. Carrasco’s

17        testimony in support of stipulation and the modified Rate No. 42 attached to it were

18        not consistent with the stipulated removal of the demand charge provisions. They

19        agreed that he would seek to withdraw his testimony and exhibit at the hearing.

20        However, they also proposed further changes to the super off-peak charges for some

21        of the rate classes affected by Rate No. 42.

22

                                               14
                                   DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                    RICHARD HANWAY
                                NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


1    Q.   HOW WERE THE VARIOUS VERSIONS OF PROPOSED CHANGES TO

2         RATE NO. 42 RESOLVED?

3    A.   At the start of the hearing on July 21, 2021, the stipulating parties agreed to resolve

4         the confusion by agreeing to remove any request to modify Rate No. 42 from Case

5         No. 20-00241-UT. This meant that the version of Rate No. 42 that had been

6         approved by the Commission as part of the final order in the general rate

 7        proceeding, Case No. 20-00104-UT, would remain in effect. After the hearing, the

 8        hearing examiner ordered the stipulating parties to file a revised Transportation

 9        Electrification Plan and tariffs that removed references to Rate No. 42. They did

10        so, and the Commission ultimately adopted a certification of stipulation that merely

11        incorporated the Rate No. 42 reporting requirements from Case No. 20-00104-UT

12        into the requirements for EPE’s bi-annual Transportation Electrification Plan

13        reports.

14

15   Q.   HAS EPE SUBSEQUENTLY PROPOSED REVISIONS TO RATE NO. 42?

16   A.   EPE has not proposed revisions to Rate No. 42 in its two subsequent Transportation

17        Electrification Plan applications, in NMPRC Docket Nos. 23-00231-UT and 26-

18        0000133. The latter case is pending. Therefore, unlike in 2021, there are no

19        concurrent dockets relating to Rate No. 42. The only issues are the ones presented

20        in this general rate case.

21

22   Q.   HAS RATE NO. 42 CHANGED AT ALL SINCE JULY 2021?

                                                15
                                   DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                    RICHARD HANWAY
                                NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1   A.    Some of the charges under Rate No. 42 changed slightly in January 2024. I

 2         understand that all of EPE’s rates were adjusted to a very small degree after an

 3         appeal of the 2020 rate case was resolved. The customer charge and the super off-

 4         peak energy charge remained the same; the on-peak energy charge declined

 5         minutely, and the off-peak energy rates for the summer and non-summer periods

 6         rose by fractions of a cent per kWh. Of course, over the years and even from month

 7         to month, the various rate riders that the Transit department pays along with other

 8         EPE customers have changed.

 9

10   VI.   EPE’S PROPOSED CHANGES TO RATE NO. 42

11   Q.    IS THE TRANSIT DEPARTMENT OPPOSED TO ANY CHANGES IN

12         RATE NO. 42?

13   A.    No.    We understand that inflationary costs will happen and do not oppose a

14         reasonable increase in the base rate charges for on-peak, off-peak, and support off-

15         peak service, if supported by the evidence in the rate case. Changing the entire

16         model of how we are charged is unreasonable, however.

17

18   Q.    WHY DOES THE CITY OPPOSE A DEMAND CHARGE FOR RATE NO.

19         42?

20   A.    When the City first approached EPE with our plan to go to electric buses, they said

21         that there would be no demand charges if we charged in the super off-peak or off-

22         peak charge windows. We have planned our new facility and our transit operations

                                               16
                                  DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                   RICHARD HANWAY
                               NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1        around that principle, opting to use a single metering point for eleven chargers

 2        serving eleven buses. We carefully schedule the bus charging to be within the super

 3        off-peak period as much as possible and within the off-peak period when we cannot

 4        accomplish full charging during the super off-peak periods. The few times in which

 5        our buses have charged during the on-peak period were, frankly, mistakes. Transit

 6        personnel are trained to be conscientious about EPE’s peak period windows, and

 7        when they fail to do so, they are reminded. In fact, my review of EPE bills indicates

 8        that on-peak charging has occurred when BYD had service mechanics on site doing

 9        warranty work and Transit department personnel are not present. The BYD

10        mechanics are not as well attuned to our charging schedule, which is driven by Rate

11        No. 42.

12

13   Q.   HOW MUCH OF TRANSIT’S CHARGING OCCURS DURING EACH

14        PERIOD OF RATE NO. 42?

15   A.   Our operations have us charging approximately 55 percent in the super off-peak

16        period and approximately 45 percent in the off-peak period.

17

18   Q.   WHY DOESN’T THE CITY ARRANGE ITS CHARGING SCHEDULE SO

19        THAT ALL CHARGING OCCURRED DURING THE SUPER OFF-PEAK

20        PERIOD?

21   A.   We would like to do so, if we could. However, I expect that the current pattern of

22        approximately 55 percent during super off-peak and 45 percent during off-peak will

                                               17
                                      DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                       RICHARD HANWAY
                                   NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


1         continue because the buses cannot make the whole day on one charge. We have to

2         pull vehicles during the day, charge them for a couple of hours, and put them back

3         in service to get the most usage out of the vehicles that we have. As I explained
